claims.text: The baseline alloy contains approximately 40 at% Ti, approximately 35 at% Ni, and a balance of Cr and Al.
The baseline alloy typically has a relatively coarse grain structure and few strengthening precipitates.
Introducing 5–10 at% W during melting and homogenizing near 1100°C for 2 hours will form nanoscale W-rich precipitates.
The W-rich precipitates will be coherent with the alloy matrix.
The W-rich precipitates will be uniformly dispersed throughout the alloy matrix.
W-rich precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion.
W-rich precipitates will hinder high-temperature recovery mechanisms.
Obstruction of dislocation motion will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Hindering recovery will slow creep deformation at elevated temperature.
The W-modified alloy will have greater elevated-temperature yield strength than the W-free baseline.
The W-modified alloy will have greater creep resistance than the W-free baseline.
The anticipated improvements in yield strength and creep resistance are approximately 15–20% relative to the baseline.
The proposed improvement applies over approximately 900–1000°C.
The strengthening magnitude depends on precipitate size, distribution, and thermal stability.

contradictions.description: The proposed baseline and boundary specify about 40 at% Ti, and the boundary permits 35–40 at% Ni, although the governing HEA definition requires every constituent to be within 5–35 at%. Thus part or all of the stated composition space violates the requested compositional definition.

The hypothesis adds 5–10 at% W without identifying which baseline elements are reduced or giving renormalized modified compositions. Retaining the stated baseline percentages while adding W would exceed 100 at%, so the base-to-modified composition is internally underdetermined.
